When Bosnia and Herzegovina held general elections last month, it  used  biometric voter identification and ballot scanners — a reform widely praised for producing fast and accurate results. That’s a real achievement. But the region’s digital foundations remain fragile, and the region’s adversaries know it. The Balkan chessboard remains checkered, torn between attraction to the European Union and to Russia, with China maneuvering for leverage. Bosnian nationalists, including separatist, pro-Russian Serbs,  won  the recent vote. But Serbs  gave  a pro-European student-led movement a clear majority in another October election, while Montenegro and Albania  closed chapters  in their EU accession talks.  The cheapest way to shift the balance of power is to undermine trust in the ballot. For the region, cybersecurity is not a technical issue. It is a strategic one. Washington is waking up to the risk — but needs to increase its focus on digital dangers. The EU is already pressing for action but must also increase its scrutiny.  Across the region, national cyber-response teams remain small and underfunded, public systems are outdated, and responsibility is fragmented. Large volumes of sensitive data, from tax and health records to the new biometric voter data in Bosnia, are held in databases that are rarely audited.  Telecommunications and surveillance networks rely on Chinese equipment. Belgrade’s Chinese-supplied “ safe city ” facial-recognition system represents the best-known example. Kremlin-funded media and anonymous networks are ready to amplify disinformation, which artificial intelligence now makes cheap to produce in local languages. China’s Huawei remains the dominant supplier to Bosnia’s two largest mobile operators, BH Telecom and Republika Srpska’s M:Tel. The security risks of that choice have never been seriously considered. Western money paid for much of that infrastructure. Bosnia’s biometric voting carries its citizens’ calls, data, and biometric records — and it is only as trustworthy as the equipment and the vendors deployed. For a hostile power, this represents an attractive environment. It does not need to defeat Balkan institutions, only to find the least-protected one. Access gained can be used to collect data on officials, NATO personnel, and diaspora communities; to map energy grids and transport hubs; and to prepare disruption that can be switched on in a crisis. Consider Albania. Earlier this year, HomeLand Justice, a hacker group that the Albanian government links to Iran,  broke  into the national parliament, deleted data, and published lawmakers’ emails on Telegram. Investigators believe the attackers had administrative access well before they revealed themselves; passwords had reportedly not been changed for years, and intrusion alarms did not sound. It was the group’s third major attack on Albanian institutions since 2022.  There are other notable attacks. Ransomware paralyzed Montenegro’s government networks in 2022. Bosnia lacks a fully functioning state-level cyber emergency response team. A 2022 ransomware attack crippled the country’s Parliamentary Assembly, taking its servers, website, and email offline. Thousands of employees in state institutions were locked out of their networks for more than two weeks. No public report on the incident or its lessons was ever released . The pattern persists. In early 2024, hackers breached the Bosnian Republika Srpska’s health information system and its tax administration. Washington has started to worry. Representatives Ritchie Torres and Joe Wilson have introduced H.R. 10748 , the Balkans Security Cooperation Act, which asks the Pentagon to report on every Western Balkan country’s security cooperation with Russia, China, the US, and NATO, including arms deals, exercises, agreements, and intelligence ties. It also asks for an assessment of the Russian-Serbian Humanitarian Center in Niš, which has signed a new development plan with Serbia’s interior ministry for 2025-2027 and whose request for diplomatic status for its staff the US and EU have resisted since 2014. The bill counts tanks, missiles, and agreements. It does not count code, vendors, or data. That gap matters, because the most likely next attack on a Balkan state will not arrive by air. As the bill moves forward, Congress should add a cyber and data annex covering four questions: Which hostile cyber operations have targeted each country since 2012, and by whom? Which foreign vendors supply critical telecommunications, energy, surveillance, and election systems, and under what legal obligations to their home governments? How well are sensitive government and citizen data protected, including biometric data? Where would US, NATO, and EU assistance close gaps fastest? Iran, whose operations in Albania are well-documented, should be included alongside Russia and China. Europe should not wait for Washington. The EU already demands cybersecurity and data protection standards as part of the accession process, and Montenegro and Albania are moving quickly through the chapters. Brussels and NATO should make cyber-resilience a visible, funded priority across the region: shared incident response, regular audits of critical databases, support for election security, and clear rules on high-risk vendors in critical networks. The new political moment creates an opening. Serbia’s incoming government has promised transparency and the rule of law while keeping military neutrality. Cyber cooperation is one area where it can work closely with EU and NATO partners without changing that stance. Bosnia’s successful use of election technology shows what is possible, and also creates a new duty to protect biometric data. Western Balkan citizens want accountable institutions. Protecting that legitimacy means protecting their networks. Dr. Emir Kremić  is a cybersecurity strategist and AI & data governance expert.   He is the former head of the Federal Institute of Statistics of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Co-Founder of Auroris AI. zh_title: 挪威稀土公司同意斥资 2700 万美元建造 Fen 试点工厂

content:
私人控股开发商稀土挪威公司批准建造一座耗资 2400 万欧元（合 2700 万美元）的试点工厂，以测试其 Fen 项目材料的加工，推动将欧洲记录在案的最大稀土矿床转变为永磁原料来源的努力。该公司周二表示，该工厂位于奥斯陆西南约 160 公里处的 Ulefoss，计划于 2027 年第三季度开始运营。资金包括来自挪威创新署的 540 万欧元和来自 Telemark 发展基金的 190 万欧元。其他贡献没有具体说明。挪威稀土公司首席执行官 Håvard Moe 在声明中表示：“这项投资是 Fen 矿床投入生产的具体步骤。” “该试点项目将使我们能够验证我们的加工路线，生成必要的运营数据，并向欧洲合作伙伴提供稀土产品，以进行金属和磁铁的测试生产。”这项投资的消息传出之际，欧盟（EU）成员国正在加大力度减少对中国稀土和磁铁的依赖。 Fen 拥有钕和镨这两种稀土元素，用于电动汽车、风力涡轮机和国防设备的强力磁铁，使该项目在挪威以外具有重要意义。总部位于柏林的 EIT RawMaterials 财团首席执行官 Bernd Schäfer 在声明中表示：“欧洲对进口稀土的依赖是我们不能再忽视的战略弱点。”
EIT 是欧盟支持的原材料创新网络，正在为挪威项目提供资金。挪威稀土综合路线的目标是在 2030 年代初期开始商业化开采稀土。在此之前，该试点工厂将测试从矿石到稀土氧化物的综合路线，生成运行数据并向欧洲合作伙伴提供产品，用于金属和磁铁的试生产。它将坐落在现有的工业建筑内。 3 月份发布的芬矿资源更新概述了 1.23 亿吨稀土氧化物品位 1.35%，其中氧化物含量约为 170 万吨。推断资源量10.8亿吨，品位1.31%，其中储量1420万吨。该资源的生效日期为 12 月 31 日。所含氧化物总量比 2024 年报告的 880 万吨增加了约 80%。该估计还确定了芬的第一个指示资源，该类别比推断材料具有更大的地质信心。钕和镨氧化物约占指定类别稀土氧化物总量的 19%。此次扩张反映了挪威稀土公司拟议采矿方法的额外钻探和变化。该公司分析了约 30,000 米的钻芯，其中包括去年勘探活动中的 10,000 米。其设计将地下开口与地表之间的保护岩层从 25 米增加到 100 米。
国家利益挪威政府于4月接管了分区程序，因为该开发涉及国家利​​益问题。9月，政府设定了到2028年完成该计划的目标，最好是在明年年底。该过程将确定地下采矿、加工设施、尾矿储存和基础设施的位置和条件。挪威环境局 3 月份发布的试点申请设想在三年内加工 6,000 吨矿石，以优化精矿生产。

【原文 English Original】
Privately held developer Rare Earths Norway approved construction of a €24-million ($27 million) pilot plant to test processing of material from its Fen project, advancing efforts to turn Europe’s largest documented rare earths deposit into a source of permanent-magnet ingredients. The facility in Ulefoss, about 160 km southwest of Oslo, is scheduled to start operating in the third quarter of 2027, the company said Tuesday . Funding includes €5.4 million from Innovation Norway and €1.9 million from the Telemark Development Fund. Other contributions weren’t specified. “This investment is a concrete step towards bringing the Fen deposit into production,” Rare Earths Norway CEO Håvard Moe said in the statement. “The pilot will allow us to validate our processing route, generate essential operating data and supply rare earth products to European partners for test production of metal and magnets.” News of the investment comes as European Union (EU) member countries step up efforts to cut their dependence on Chinese rare earths and magnets. Fen holds neodymium and praseodymium – two rare earth elements that are used in powerful magnets for electric vehicles, wind turbines and defence equipment, giving the project significance beyond Norway. “Europe’s dependence on imported rare earths is a strategic vulnerability we can no longer afford to ignore,” Bernd Schäfer, CEO of the Berlin-based EIT RawMaterials consortium, said in the statement. EIT, an EU-backed raw materials innovation network, is providing funding for the Norwegian project. Integrated route Rare Earths Norway aims to begin extracting rare earths commercially in the early 2030s. Until then, the pilot plant will test an integrated route from ore to rare earth oxides, generate operating data and supply products to European partners for trial production of metals and magnets. It will sit inside an existing industrial building. A resource update for Fen released in March outlined 123 million indicated tonnes grading 1.35% total rare earth oxides, containing about 1.7 million tonnes of oxides. Inferred resources totalled 1.08 billion tonnes grading 1.31%, containing 14.2 million tonnes. The resource has an effective Dec. 31 date. Combined contained oxides rose about 80% from the 8.8 million tonnes reported in 2024. The estimate also established Fen’s first indicated resource, a category carrying greater geological confidence than inferred material. Neodymium and praseodymium oxides account for about 19% of total rare earth oxides in the indicated category. The expansion reflected additional drilling and changes to Rare Earths Norway’s proposed mining approach. The company had analysed about 30,000 metres of drill core, including 10,000 metres from last year’s exploration campaign. Its design increased the protective rock layer between underground openings and the surface to 100 metres from 25 metres. National interest Norway’s government took over the zoning process in April because the development involves matters of national interest. In September, the government set an ambition to complete the plan by 2028, preferably by the end of next year. The process will determine locations and conditions for underground mining, processing facilities, tailings storage and infrastructure. A pilot application published by Norway’s Environment Agency in March envisaged processing 6,000 tonnes of ore over three years to optimize concentrate production.

content:
发言人办公室对古巴政权的对外军事支持和非法收入网络的进一步制裁 - 情况说明书 情况说明书 2026 年 11 月 5 日 今天，美国国务院指定了 8 个实体和 2 名个人，并将 5 艘船只确定为封锁财产，以进一步推动特朗普政府全面推动结束古巴政权在古巴和整个半球的恶意活动。这一行动包括与古巴政权的石油运输网络、古巴精英、国有进口和技术支持实体以及该政权军队的中国供应商相关的目标。今天制裁的所有国务院目标都是根据第 14404 号行政命令 (E.O.) 指定的，该命令授权对符合与古巴镇压以及对美国国家安全和外交政策的其他威胁有关的特定标准的外国人实施制裁。此外，今天，财政部外国资产控制办公室 (OFAC) 主任根据 E.O. 发布了一项决定。第 14404 号法令授权对任何在古巴经济的制造、技术、电子和海洋部门经营或曾经经营的外国人实施制裁。这些新部门的确定针对的是该政权及其支持者，而不是古巴人民。
美国继续授权人道主义贸易，包括食品、药品和医疗设备，并支持信息向古巴人民自由流动。 古巴政权的非法收入网络 古巴的统治精英囤积岛上的能源和航运资源以图谋取私利，使古巴人民面临停电、燃料短缺和经济停滞的困境。为了维持该系统的运行，该政权依赖离岸中介机构网络。今天，美国国务院正在指定为古巴政权运送原油和石油产品的广泛航运网络的一部分。 GUILLERMO FAUSTINO RODRIGUEZ LOPEZ CALLEJA (GUILLERMO) 是往返古巴运输石油产品的广泛海运公司网络的一部分。 GUILLERMO 是根据第 2 节指定的。 E.O. 2(a)(i)(A) 14404 从事或曾经从事古巴经济能源部门的工作。 CAROIL TRANSPORT MARINE LTD (CAROIL) 是一家总部位于塞浦路斯的公司，管理着悬挂古巴国旗的原油油轮，这些油轮在古巴运输能源产品。财政部此前根据 E.O. 于 2019 年 9 月 24 日指定 CAROIL。 13850. CAROIL 根据第 13850 条被指定。 E.O. 2(a)(i)(A) 14404 从事或曾经从事古巴经济能源部门的工作。以下船舶被确定为 CAROIL 拥有权益的财产： ESPERANZA (IMO: 9289166)：CAROIL 是商业管理者。
